why: Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching is a domain-specific model of teachers' professional knowledge and an assessment framework, not a general theory of how people learn or are taught.

This is a single university course implementation for a specific population and setting, delivered through BESMART and evaluated with course-specific assessments, rather than a reusable instructional element.

The MKID laboratory is a setting-specific example of Hands-on Learning because students directly operate specialized equipment, develop acquisition tools, and analyze experimental data; its apparatus requirements are implementation conditions rather than a distinct instructional element.
This is a physics detection principle explaining how an MKID converts absorbed photons into a microwave readout signal, not a general theory of learning, an educational product, or a research method.
